# SUMMARY & LOGIC:
This code tests whether missing data meets Missing At Random (MAR) assumptions 
required for multiple imputation.

Strategy:

1. Quantify overall missingness rates
2. Test for systematic patterns:
   - Survey fatigue (missingness ~ study day)
   - Person effects (missingness ~ participant)
   - Correlated missingness (variables missing together)
   - Predictive relationships (observed predictors ~ missingness)*

MAR requires: missingness can depend on observed data but not unobserved values.

*Tests use logistic regression to check if observed morning variables predict 
evening outcome missingness, controlling for person and time effects.

# Missingness Rate

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Define variables used in Q1/Q2 models
model_vars <- c("alias",                      # Participant ID
                "evening_interference",        # Outcome: actual interference
                "interf_worry",               # Predictor: worry about interference
                "morning_mood", "morning_pain", "morning_stress",  # Confounders
                "daily_avg_stress", "daily_avg_pain", "daily_avg_mood",
                "Age",
                "day_count")                  # Study day

# Visual missingness patterns by participant
vis_miss(data_set_b4mice %>% 
           select(all_of(model_vars)) %>% 
           filter(day_count > 0) %>%  # Exclude day 0 (equipment induction)
           group_by(alias) %>% 
           arrange(day_count)) + 
  facet_wrap(~ alias) + 
  labs(caption = "Missingness: count by day, facets show detail across Participants") 

# Overall missingness pattern
vis_miss(data_set_b4mice %>% 
           select(all_of(model_vars)) %>% 
           filter(day_count > 0) %>%
           arrange(day_count)) +
  labs(caption = "Missingness: count by day") 

# Complete case analysis summary
# Rule of thumb: ≥80% complete cases supports ~5 imputations (White et al. 2010)
data_set_b4mice %>%
  select(all_of(model_vars)) %>% 
  filter(day_count > 0) %>%
  mutate(complete_case = complete.cases(.)) %>%
  summarise(
    n_total = n(),
    n_complete = sum(complete_case),
    n_incomplete = sum(!complete_case),
    pct_incomplete = (n_incomplete/n_total)*100,
    pct_complete = (n_complete/n_total)*100
  ) %>% kable()
```

# Summary Table

```{r}
# Variable-level missingness rates
missingness_summary <- data_set_b4mice %>%
  select(all_of(model_vars)) %>% 
  filter(day_count > 0) %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~mean(is.na(.)) * 100)) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "pct_missing") %>%
  arrange(desc(pct_missing))

missingness_summary %>% kable()
```

## MAR Assumption Tests


### Missingness ~ time

Here we explore temporal dropout patterns. The expectation under MCAR is that 
missingness rates will be stable over time. We examine this chart looking for:

1. Upward trends in % missing as study day increases (survey fatigue)
2. Systematic differences between early vs late study periods

Under MCAR, we would expect to see no clear trends in either case, with only 
random day-to-day fluctuation in missingness rates.

```{r}
# Test 1: Survey fatigue (missingness increases over time?)
missingness_by_day <- data_set_b4mice %>%
  select(all_of(model_vars)) %>% 
  filter(day_count > 0) %>%
  group_by(day_count) %>%
  summarise(
    pct_missing_worry = mean(is.na(interf_worry)) * 100,
    pct_missing_interference = mean(is.na(evening_interference)) * 100,
    pct_missing_pain = mean(is.na(morning_pain)) * 100
  )

# Visualize temporal trends
ggplot(missingness_by_day, aes(x = day_count)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = pct_missing_worry, color = "Worry")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = pct_missing_interference, color = "Interference")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = pct_missing_pain, color = "Pain")) +
  labs(x = "Study Day", y = "% Missing", 
       title = "Missingness Over Time (Survey Fatigue Test)")
```

### Missingness ~ Participant?

This code examines person-level heterogeneity in missingness patterns to assess whether certain participants systematically provide less data. 

Scatter plot shows relationship between worry and interference missingness:

* Points on diagonal = participants miss both equally (whole survey sessions skipped)
* Points off diagonal = differential missingness (one variable more likely missing than the other)

under MCAR we would expect a random scatter around diagonal and no systematic pattern of morning worry vs evening interference prevalence.

In the next steps glm() will test whether the levels of worry detected in the morning predict the report of interference being missingness on the same evening.

```{r}
# Test 2: Person-level differences in compliance
missingness_by_person <- data_set_b4mice %>%
  select(all_of(model_vars)) %>% 
  filter(day_count > 0) %>%
  group_by(alias) %>%
  summarise(
    n_days = n(),
    pct_missing_worry = mean(is.na(interf_worry)) * 100,
    pct_missing_interference = mean(is.na(evening_interference)) * 100,
    pct_any_missing = mean(is.na(interf_worry) | is.na(evening_interference)) * 100
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(pct_any_missing))

missingness_by_person %>% kable()

# Correlation between worry and interference missingness
ggplot(missingness_by_person, aes(x = pct_missing_worry, 
                                   y = pct_missing_interference)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = alias), vjust = -0.5, size = 3) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray") +
  labs(x = "% Missing Worry",
       y = "% Missing Interference",
       title = "Relationship Between Missingness Types (Person-Level)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Missingness Co-occurrence?

This UpSet plot shows which combinations of variables tend to be missing together. 
Understanding co-occurrence patterns helps distinguish between item-level skipping 
(participants selectively skip certain questions) versus survey-level dropout 
(participants miss entire survey sessions).

Note: Morning mood, pain, and stress are always asked in the same morning survey, 
so these three variables will always be missing together when the morning survey is 
skipped. Similarly, evening interference and morning worry come from different survey 
sessions (evening and morning respectively), so their co-occurrence patterns reflect 
between-survey rather than within-survey missingness.

```{r warning=F}
# Test 3: Which variables tend to be missing together?
# UpSet plot shows combinations of missing variables
gg_miss_upset(data_set_b4mice %>%
              select(all_of(model_vars)) %>%
              filter(day_count > 0))
```

### Outcome Missing ~ Predictors

This section tests the core MAR assumption: whether observed variables predict 
missingness patterns. We create binary indicators for whether each key variable 
is missing, then use logistic regression to test if observed morning states 
predict the probability of missing data.

**MAR vs MCAR distinction**: 
- MCAR requires missingness to be completely independent of all variables (observed and unobserved)
- MAR allows missingness to depend on observed data, but not on the unobserved values themselves

This means that if data is MAR missingness depends on observed data (lagged/same-day observables), 
but not on unobserved/missing values conditional on those observables.


```{r}
# Create binary missingness indicators for logistic regression
Missngness_glm_DF <- data_set_b4mice %>%
              select(all_of(model_vars)) %>%
              filter(day_count > 0) %>%
              mutate(interference_missing = is.na(evening_interference),
                     worry_missing = is.na(interf_worry))
```

#### Interference Missing ~ Observed Predictors

*Test:**Does morning worry predict evening interference being missing?**

This tests whether morning worry (net of pain/mood/stress) predicts evening 
interference missingness. 

* Significant worry → supports MAR (high morning worry → skip evening → imputation conditions on observed worry and other morning states).
* Non-significant → supports MCAR.


```{r}
# Test 4a: Do observed morning states predict evening interference missingness?
# MAR allows this; MCAR would require no relationship
missingness_model_1 <- glm(
  interference_missing ~ morning_pain + morning_stress + 
    morning_mood + interf_worry +day_count ,
  family = binomial,
  data = Missngness_glm_DF
)

summary(missingness_model_1)



```

#### Worry Missing ~ Observed Predictors

**Do observed lagged states predict morning worry data being missing?**
This tests whether previous states predict morning survey non-completion (which 
includes worry). 

* If lagged worry/pain/mood/stress predict missingness → supports for MAR imputation can succesfully condition on them). 
* If lagged worry/pain/mood/stress do not predict missingness → supports for MCAR. 

```{r}
# Test 4b: Do observed morning states predict worry missingness?
Missingness_model_2b <- glm(
  worry_missing ~ lag(interf_worry) + 
    lag(evening_interference) + 
    lag(daily_avg_pain) + lag(daily_avg_stress) + lag(daily_avg_mood) + 
    day_count,
  family = binomial,
  data = Missngness_glm_DF
)


summary(Missingness_model_2b)
```


Lagged prior-day worry significantly predicted higher morning worry missingness (OR=1.35, p=.008), while prior pain marginally predicted lower missingness (OR=0.79, p=.061). This supports MAR: imputation conditions on these observed lagged states to adjust for systematic patterns


## MAR-based sensitivity analysis
[Text copied from Q2 supplementary to complement the exploration, please see Q2 supplementary for more details]

Our MAR diagnostics revealed that lagged worry (t-1) significantly predicted 
current worry missingness ($\beta=0.30$, p=.008), suggesting imputation models should 
ideally condition on this predictor. To assess robustness to this MAR pattern, 
we compared Q2 model estimates under two imputation strategies:

* **Model A**: Two-level PMM without lagged worry predictor (primary specification)
* **Model B**: Two-level PMM including lagged worry predictor (MAR-informed)

|term                       | est_A|  se_A|  lwr_A| upr_A|   | est_B|  se_B|  lwr_B| upr_B|
|:--------------------------|-----:|-----:|------:|-----:|:-:|-----:|-----:|------:|-----:|
|(Intercept)                |  1.37| 0.862| -0.325| 3.065|   |  1.35| 0.935| -0.487| 3.188|
|lagged_interf_worry        |  0.28| 0.058|  0.167| 0.394|   |  0.26| 0.061|  0.143| 0.382|
|lagged_worry_outcome_error | -0.08| 0.044| -0.169| 0.005|   | -0.08| 0.046| -0.172| 0.009|
|lagged_pain_trend_3d       | -0.08| 0.076| -0.233| 0.064|   | -0.11| 0.081| -0.269| 0.048|
|lagged_mood_trend_3d       |  0.18| 0.107| -0.031| 0.390|   |  0.19| 0.118| -0.040| 0.425|
|lagged_stress_trend_3d     |  0.19| 0.071|  0.051| 0.329|   |  0.20| 0.076|  0.047| 0.345|
|day_count                  |  0.01| 0.009| -0.009| 0.024|   |  0.00| 0.010| -0.015| 0.022|
|Age_c                      | -0.01| 0.033| -0.072| 0.057|   | -0.01| 0.031| -0.067| 0.053|

The pooled fixed‑effect estimates from the analysis model were highly similar across the two imputation strategies (See table above). For all parameters, point estimates, standard errors, and confidence intervals overlapped closely. In particular, the lagged morning interference coefficient remained positive and of comparable magnitude in both models (Model A: 0.28, 95% CI [0.17, 0.39]; Model B: 0.26, 95% CI [0.14, 0.38]), and the pattern of results for the lagged symptom trends, day count, and age was essentially unchanged.The maximum difference in point estimates across any parameter was 0.03 (lagged pain trend), 

representing <5% relative change. Considering these findings, our longitudinal inferences are appear robust to reasonable variation in the imputation model for morning worry nd we therefore selected the more parsimonious and numerically stable imputation model without the lagged term as our primary specification.
